passages.t: Remember, O LORD: life under foreign rule
passages.happening:
The last poem is the whole community praying. ‘Remember, O LORD, what has happened to us’ (verse 1). “Look and see our disgrace!” (verse 1).

Then they tell God what life is like now. ‘Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners’ (verse 2). ‘We have become fatherless orphans; our mothers are widows’ (verse 3). ‘We must buy the water we drink; our wood comes at a price’ (verse 4). They are hunted and weary and find no rest (verse 5).

They look back over their history. ‘We submitted to Egypt and Assyria to get enough bread’ (verse 6). ‘Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment’ (verse 7). ‘Slaves rule over us; there is no one to deliver us from their hands’ (verse 8). They risk their lives for bread because of raiders in the wilderness (verse 9), and their skin burns with the fever of hunger (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
This poem looks at life some time after the fall. The people who stayed in Judah lived under Babylonian control. Their family land, which God's law meant to stay in each family for good, had gone to strangers. To the first hearers that was more than a loss of property. The land was an inheritance from God, a share in his promise, and they had lost it.

Water from wells and wood from the hills had once been free to the people of the land. Paying for them was a mark of subjection. Orphans and widows were the most exposed people in any ancient society, and now the whole nation is in their place. The slaves who rule them in verse 8 are probably the officials of the Babylonian administration, servants of a foreign king, spoken of with contempt.

Verse 6 looks back over the whole history of the kingdom. For generations Israel and Judah had sought safety in alliances, now with Assyria, now with Egypt, instead of trusting the LORD. Verse 7 voices the feeling that the generation of the exile was paying for centuries of unfaithfulness before it.

The acrostic is gone. The poem still has twenty-two verses, the number of the Hebrew letters, but the lines do not follow the alphabet. It is as though the strength to shape grief from A to Z has run out, while the shape remains.
passages.later: The prophets had warned against the alliances verse 6 regrets: ‘calling out to Egypt, then turning to Assyria’ (Hosea 7:11). Jeremiah and Ezekiel both take up the complaint of verse 7 and answer it. Jeremiah promises a day when ‘each will die for his own iniquity’ (Jeremiah 31:30), and Ezekiel says, ‘A son will not bear the iniquity of his father’ (Ezekiel 18:20).
passages.hard:
‘Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment’ (verse 7). Does God punish children for their parents' sins?

The verse is a cry, not a doctrine. It says what the people felt: they were living in the ruins their ancestors' choices had made. That was true in a plain sense. A nation's choices shape the lives of its children. But the Bible does not leave the complaint unanswered. The law already said that ‘each is to die for his own sin’ (Deuteronomy 24:16), and both Jeremiah and Ezekiel take up this very proverb and reject it as a description of how God judges (Jeremiah 31:29-30; Ezekiel 18). The same poem also says, a few verses later, that the people themselves have sinned (verse 16).

No reader should take from this verse that a child's suffering is a punishment for a parent's sin. It is a people's honest cry from the ruins, and Scripture answers it.
passages.asks: The people ask God to remember, which in the Bible means to act in faithfulness. Ask what you would want God to remember and see in your own life or community. And ask what burdens you carry that were made by others' choices, and whether you have brought them to God as honestly as this.

passages.t: Violence, shame, and joy turned to mourning
passages.happening:
The list goes on, and it grows darker. Women and young women have been violated in Zion and in the towns of Judah (verse 11). ‘Princes have been hung up by their hands; elders receive no respect’ (verse 12). ‘Young men toil at millstones; boys stagger under loads of wood’ (verse 13).

‘The elders have left the city gate; the young men have stopped their music’ (verse 14). ‘Joy has left our hearts; our dancing has turned to mourning’ (verse 15).

Then comes confession: “The crown has fallen from our head. Woe to us, for we have sinned!” (verse 16). Because of this their hearts are faint and their eyes grow dim, ‘because of Mount Zion, which lies desolate, patrolled by foxes’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
These verses name the cruelties of conquest: women violated, princes hung up by their hands, the elders shamed, the young forced into slave labor. The poem names them in a line each and does not describe them. These notes do the same.

Grinding grain at the millstone was the work of slaves and women, so young men made to grind were being publicly humiliated, as Samson was by the Philistines. The city gate was where the elders sat to judge disputes, do business and give counsel. It was the center of public life. Its emptiness means the community's order has collapsed.

The crown of verse 16 is the people's honor and the kingdom itself, now fallen. And the foxes, or jackals, walking over Mount Zion suggest that some time has passed since the destruction. The hill where the temple stood is now a place for wild animals.

The confession in verse 16 matters. The people do not only say that their fathers sinned. They say ‘we have sinned’ of themselves. The first hearers were given words that hold their own guilt and their grief together.
passages.later: The exiles in Babylon sang the same grief: ‘By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion’ (Psalm 137:1). A psalm of thanks later prays the reverse of verse 15: ‘You turned my mourning into dancing’ (Psalm 30:11). And Zechariah, after the return, hears the LORD say, ‘I will return to Jerusalem with mercy’ (Zechariah 1:16).
passages.hard:
The poem names the rape of women and young women in a single verse. How should a reader take it?

The verse is a lament. It tells God what was done to the people, and it calls it what it was: a disgrace and a horror, part of the cruelty of an invading army. It does not blame the women, and it does not treat what was done to them as their shame. It lays it before God among the wrongs he is asked to remember and see.

Nothing in this chapter makes such violence anything other than evil, then or now.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The people list their losses and then confess their own sin. Ask whether you can grieve what others did to you and still be honest about your own wrongs, without letting either cancel the other. And ask what joy you have lost that you need to name before God.

passages.t: The LORD reigns forever, and a prayer to be restored
passages.happening:
Then the people look up. ‘You, O LORD, reign forever; Your throne endures from generation to generation’ (verse 19).

On that ground they ask the hardest question. ‘Why have You forgotten us forever? Why have You forsaken us for so long?’ (verse 20).

And they pray: ‘Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return; renew our days as of old’ (verse 21).

The book ends with a fear: ‘unless You have utterly rejected us and remain angry with us beyond measure’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
David's throne has fallen, and the temple lies in ruins. But God's throne has not been touched by Babylon's victory. That confession is what makes the prayer possible. The people do not pray because their circumstances have changed. They pray because God still reigns.

The word return in verse 21 is shuv in Hebrew, and it is used twice in the line, once for God's restoring and once for the people's return. The same word is used for God bringing his people back and for the people turning back to God. The prayer asks God to act first. Turning back to him is itself something he must give. The words ‘renew our days as of old’ ask for the relationship God once had with his people to be made new, which echoes chapter 3's mercies that are new every morning.

The last verse is hard to translate. It can be read as an open condition, unless God has utterly rejected them; as a question, whether he has; or as a concession, even though he has. On every reading, the book ends with a prayer still waiting for an answer.

When Lamentations is read aloud in the synagogue, verse 21 is repeated after verse 22, so that the last word the congregation hears is the request to be restored. The same custom applies to a few other books with hard endings.
passages.later: A psalm prays the same prayer: ‘Restore us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved’ (Psalm 80:3). Another confesses, ‘But You, O LORD, sit enthroned forever’ (Psalm 102:12). And Jeremiah carries the LORD's answer to the fear of verse 22: ‘For I will restore them from captivity and will have compassion on them’ (Jeremiah 33:26).
passages.hard:
Why would the Bible end a book with the fear that God has rejected his people?

Many readers find the ending unsettling, and it is meant to be. On any reading of verse 22, the book leaves the community praying without an answer. That honesty is part of its gift. Scripture includes a prayer that has not yet been answered, which shows that faith can keep speaking to God in the gap between the promise and its fulfillment.

The Jewish custom of repeating verse 21 expresses the same faith from another side: the last word is the request to be restored. And the rest of the Old Testament answers the question with the prophets' promises of return and with the return itself, told in Ezra and Nehemiah.

If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The book ends with a prayer that has no answer yet. Ask what it might mean for your own prayers that Scripture includes one like this. And ask what you could say to God on the ground of verse 19 when you cannot yet see an answer.
